newsitem.title: PERU: Peru hostage crisis talks set for Tuesday.
newsitem.headline: Peru hostage crisis talks set for Tuesday.

text.p: Marxist MRTA rebels holding 72 hostages at the Japanese ambassador's residence in Lima and the government of President Alberto Fujimori are ready to return to negotiations to end Peru's two-month hostage crisis.

Fujimori announced on Sunday during a visit to London that Tupac Amaru Revolutionary Movement (MRTA) leader Nestor Cerpa Cartolini's lieutenant Roli Rojas, known by his nom de guerre "El Arabe" (The Arab), would meet the government's negotiator Domingo Palermo, Peruvian education minister, on Tuesday.

"At this preliminary stage it is Cerpa Cartolino's number two who will be the interlocutor of Minister Palermo," he said. "We hope the preliminary talks will make enough progress to enter definitive talks, probably with Cerpa Cartolini himself."

The rebels, who stormed the Japanese residence on Dec. 17 and seized hundreds of guests at a cocktail party, have not talked with the government face-to-face since Dec. 28, when Palermo met Cerpa, a 43-year-old former textile worker.

Since then the 15 rebels have released hundreds of captives, but kept their most prized captives who include the ambassadors of Japan and Bolivia, Peruvian government ministers, Japanese and local businessmen and Fujimori's own brother, Pedro.
Fujimori, the son of Japanese immigrants, has refused to discuss the MRTA's main demand -- the release of about 400 jailed comrades -- and the siege has become a tense stand-off.

But a breakthrough came late last week when Roman Catholic Bishop Juan Luis Cipriani and two other negotiators came out of the residence saying there was a good chance of preliminary conversations to seek a definitive solution to the siege.

Fujimori came under pressure for a peaceful outcome when he met Japanese Prime Minister Ryutaro Hashimoto last weekend. The Peruvian leader told Reuters in London: "We will exhaust all possible avenues to ensure that the hostages are freed without the use of force."
"I am optimistic that I will succeed in releasing all the hostages safe and in good health," he said in the interview.

There is speculation of asylum abroad for the rebels, but Fujimori said: "We haven't had success finding a country where they could seek asylum. It is quite a complex situation and in this moment there are few countries willing to have them."

While concern in Lima was centred over the weekend on the health of the hostages, some of whom are said by relatives to need urgent medical care despite doctors' visits organised by the Red Cross, preparations have quietly gone ahead for talks.

Fujimori said they would take place in a house rented by the government under the auspices of the Red Cross, the Vatican and guarantor countries Japan and Canada. He also referred to a blue Chevrolet van parked down the road from the residence that will be used to transport the MRTA negotiator to the talks.

Security around the residence is tight, with armed police cordons around the building and sharpshooters on roofs, backed up by armoured personnel carriers. Local residents are being issued with identity cards similar to those issued to press.

Police and the rebels continued their musical psychological warfare during the weekend, with huge police speakers blasting the residence with patriotic "criolla" folk music and the rebels chanting back revolutionary hymns and slogans.

Fujimori has earned plaudits from world leaders including U.S. President Bill Clinton for his tough stance on the siege, unsoftened by his brother and another relative being among the hostages. "I am managing with the same approach as I would with no relatives there," he said.
